case_name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
facts: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act which restricted religious mutt property ownership, challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments under Article 368.
issues: What is the extent of Parliament's amending power under Article 368?
Can Parliament abrogate or alter the fundamental structure of the Constitution?
ratio_decidendi: Parliament has wide constituent amending power under Article 368 but cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Indian Constitution. The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
verdict: Upheld 24th Amendment; partially struck down Article 31C; established the landmark Basic Structure Doctrine.
precedents_overruled: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967)

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Shankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India
facts: Landowners challenged the validity of the First Amendment, which inserted Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule, arguing it curtailed Fundamental Rights under Part III in violation of Article 13(2).
issues: Does 'law' in Article 13(2) include constitutional amendments made under Article 368?
ratio_decidendi: 'Law' in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary legislative enactments and not to constituent amendments made under Article 368. Parliament can amend any provision including Fundamental Rights.
verdict: Upheld the validity of the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan
facts: Challenge to the 17th Amendment Act which added diverse State land reform acts into the Ninth Schedule.
issues: Can Fundamental Rights be amended under Article 368?
Did the 17th Amendment require state ratification under the Article 368 proviso?
ratio_decidendi: Affirmed Shankari Prasad ruling that Parliament's amending power extends to Fundamental Rights. However, Justices Hidayatullah and Mudholkar expressed profound doubts whether Fundamental Rights could be stripped away.
verdict: Upheld 17th Amendment, but sowed the conceptual seeds for Golak Nath and Basic Structure.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: I.C. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab
acts_referred: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953
facts: Family of Golak Nath held 500 acres of land. State declared excess land surplus under land reforms act. Family challenged 17th Amendment as abridging fundamental property rights.
issues: Is a constitutional amendment a 'law' under Article 13(2)?
Can Parliament amend Part III Fundamental Rights?
ratio_decidendi: Fundamental Rights hold a transcendental and immutable position. Constitutional amendments under Article 368 are 'law' under Article 13(2). Parliament has no power to abridge Fundamental Rights. Applied Doctrine of Prospective Overruling.
verdict: Held Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; prospectively applied to save past amendments.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
facts: Allahabad High Court invalidated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's election for corrupt electoral practices. Parliament enacted the 39th Amendment inserting Article 329A(4) placing election of PM and Speaker beyond judicial review.
issues: Does Article 329A(4) violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution?
ratio_decidendi: First direct application of Basic Structure Doctrine. Democracy, rule of law, equality (Article 14), and judicial review are basic features. A constitutional amendment placing an individual's election beyond judicial scrutiny violates the Basic Structure.
verdict: Struck down Article 329A(4) inserted by the 39th Amendment; upheld election on statutory merits.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
facts: Minerva Mills challenged nationalization and the 42nd Amendment which added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 asserting unlimited amending power and expanded Article 31C to subordinate Fundamental Rights to all Directive Principles.
issues: Can Parliament grant itself unlimited amending power under Article 368?
Can Directive Principles take blanket precedence over Fundamental Rights?
ratio_decidendi: Limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot convert limited power into unlimited power. The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential basic feature.
verdict: Struck down Section 55 (Article 368(4)-(5)) and Section 4 (blanket Article 31C) of 42nd Amendment.
keywords: part iii and part iv balance

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Waman Rao v. Union of India
acts_referred: Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961
facts: Challenge to agricultural land ceiling acts included in the Ninth Schedule and the constitutional validity of Articles 31A, 31B, and 31C.
issues: Does the Basic Structure doctrine apply to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule?
What is the cutoff date for applying the Basic Structure doctrine?
ratio_decidendi: Established the April 24, 1973 cutoff date (date of Kesavananda judgment). Ninth Schedule amendments made before April 24, 1973 are valid and immune; Ninth Schedule laws enacted on or after April 24, 1973 are subject to Basic Structure judicial review.
verdict: Upheld Articles 31A, 31B, and unamended 31C; established prospective Basic Structure cutoff line.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu
facts: Referred to 9-judge bench to definitively resolve whether statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda Bharati are completely immunized from judicial review for violating Fundamental Rights.
issues: Can Parliament insulate statutes violating Fundamental Rights from judicial review by putting them in Ninth Schedule?
ratio_decidendi: All laws placed in Ninth Schedule post-April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review using the 'Rights Test' and 'Essence of Rights Test'. If a Ninth Schedule statute violates the principles underlying Articles 14, 19, or 21, it damages the Basic Structure and will be void.
verdict: Unanimously affirmed that Ninth Schedule cannot be used as a constitutional black hole to bypass the Basic Structure.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
facts: Communist leader A.K. Gopalan was detained under Preventive Detention Act without trial. He claimed detention infringed freedom of movement under Article 19(1)(d) and personal liberty under Article 21.
issues: Does 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 incorporate American 'due process'?
Are Fundamental Rights mutually exclusive silos?
ratio_decidendi: Adopted narrow literal interpretation. 'Procedure established by law' means state-enacted statutory law, not natural justice. Articles 19 and 21 operate in mutually exclusive silos; preventive detention does not attract Article 19. (Justice Fazl Ali dissented).
verdict: Upheld Preventive Detention Act; rejected substantive due process.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
facts: Regional Passport Office impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport 'in public interest' without furnishing reasons or providing a hearing.
issues: Is the right to travel abroad part of personal liberty under Article 21?
Must procedure under Article 21 satisfy principles of natural justice and Article 14 non-arbitrariness?
ratio_decidendi: Overruled Gopalan's silo approach; established the 'Golden Triangle' of Articles 14, 19, and 21. Any procedure depriving life or personal liberty must be 'just, fair, and reasonable' and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. Right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty.
verdict: Substantive and procedural due process integrated into Article 21; audi alteram partem mandated.
precedents_overruled: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
facts: Death-row convict Sunil Batra challenged solitary confinement and inhumane bar fetters in Tihar Jail prior to disposal of appeals.
issues: Do prisoners retain Fundamental Rights inside prison?
Is solitary confinement without judicial order constitutional under Article 21?
ratio_decidendi: Prison walls do not keep out Fundamental Rights. Solitary confinement and barbaric bar fetters without judicial order violate Article 21 and 14. Prisoners are entitled to humane treatment and bodily dignity.
verdict: Declared solitary confinement of convicts awaiting appeal unconstitutional; reformed prison jurisprudence.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
facts: Kapila Hingorani filed PIL highlighting tens of thousands of undertrial prisoners languishing in Bihar jails for periods exceeding maximum statutory sentences awaiting trial.
issues: Is the right to a speedy trial a fundamental right under Article 21?
Is free legal aid mandatory under Article 21 and 39A?
ratio_decidendi: Right to speedy trial is an integral fundamental right under Article 21. Depriving indigent accused of legal representation violates fair procedure. Ordered immediate release of undertrials whose detention exceeded maximum sentences.
verdict: First landmark PIL in Indian legal history; released over 40,000 undertrials; established right to speedy trial and legal aid.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
facts: British national detained under COFEPOSA was denied permission to meet family members and legal counsel under stringent prison restrictions.
issues: What is the scope of 'life' under Article 21?
Does Article 21 guarantee the right to live with human dignity?
ratio_decidendi: Article 21 guarantees something more than mere animal existence or physical survival. It includes the right to live with human dignity and all that goes with it, including bare necessities of life, nutrition, clothing, shelter, facilities for reading, and free intercourse with family.
verdict: Held harsh interview restrictions invalid; established dignity as core content of Article 21.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
facts: PIL petition letter by Executive Chairman, Legal Aid Services West Bengal, drawing attention to frequent custodial deaths and police brutality.
issues: What guidelines must be formulated to prevent custodial violence and safeguard arrested persons under Articles 21 and 22?
ratio_decidendi: Custodial violence, torture, and custodial deaths strike at the heart of the rule of law. Formulated 11 binding guidelines (memo of arrest, informing relative, medical examination every 48 hours, right to meet lawyer, display at control room) that must be strictly observed during arrest and detention.
verdict: Laid down mandatory D.K. Basu Guidelines on arrest; failure makes police officers liable for contempt of court.

case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
facts: Appellants challenged involuntary administration of neuro-scientific investigative techniques: Narco-analysis (sodium pentothal), Polygraph test (lie detector), and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP).
issues: Does involuntary narco-analysis violate self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and mental privacy under Article 21?
ratio_decidendi: Involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraphy, and brain mapping constitutes testimonial compulsion violating Article 20(3) and infringes personal liberty and mental privacy under Article 21. Tests can only be administered voluntarily with informed consent.
verdict: Declared non-consensual narco-analysis and lie detector tests unconstitutional.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India
facts: Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse at KEM Hospital Mumbai, remained in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) for 37 years following a brutal sexual assault. Journalist Pinki Virani filed a writ petition seeking withdrawal of life support.
issues: Does Article 21 encompass the right to die with dignity?
Is passive euthanasia permissible under Indian constitutional law?
ratio_decidendi: Differentiated active euthanasia (administering lethal injection, prohibited) from passive euthanasia (withholding artificial life-support). Legalized passive euthanasia subject to strict High Court approval and medical board evaluation under the parens patriae doctrine.
verdict: Permitted passive euthanasia under judicial supervision; declined withdrawal for Aruna as KEM staff wished to care for her.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India
facts: Common Cause filed PIL seeking legal recognition of 'living wills' (advance medical directives) enabling terminally ill patients to refuse artificial life prolongation.
issues: Is the right to die with dignity part of Article 21?
Are advance medical directives / living wills legally enforceable?
ratio_decidendi: Right to die with dignity is an inseparable facet of the fundamental right to live with dignity under Article 21. An adult person of sound mind has bodily autonomy to execute an Advance Medical Directive refusing artificial life support when death is imminent.
verdict: Unanimously recognized Living Wills and advance medical directives; laid down simplified procedural safeguards.

case_name: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra
facts: Search warrants issued in Dalmia Group fraud investigation. Petitioners claimed search and seizure of private documents violated Article 19(1)(f) and Article 20(3).
issues: Does the Indian Constitution guarantee a fundamental right to privacy analogous to the US Fourth Amendment?
ratio_decidendi: The Indian Constitution does not contain any fundamental right to privacy analogous to the American Fourth Amendment. Search and seizure by police is not testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
verdict: Rejected constitutional right to privacy (later overruled in Puttaswamy).

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
facts: Kharak Singh, acquitted in a dacoity case, was subjected to police surveillance: secret picketing, domiciliary night visits, and verification of movements under U.P. Police Regulations.
issues: Does police surveillance and domiciliary night visits violate fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(d) and 21?
ratio_decidendi: Majority held domiciliary night visits violate personal liberty under Article 21 (a person's house is their castle), but held privacy is not a guaranteed fundamental right. Subba Rao, J. dissented, prophetically writing that privacy is an essential ingredient of personal liberty.
verdict: Struck down night visits; majority denied comprehensive right to privacy.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (Auto Shankar Case)
facts: Condemned prisoner Auto Shankar wrote an autobiography disclosing unholy nexus with high-ranking police and prison officials. Prison authorities threatened publisher Nakkheeran with legal action to suppress publication.
issues: Does freedom of press include right to publish without pre-censorship?
What is the relationship between freedom of speech and citizen's right to privacy?
ratio_decidendi: Right to privacy is implicit in Article 21 ('right to be let alone'). A citizen has a right to safeguard the privacy of his family, marriage, procreation, and education. Public officials cannot suppress publication or claim damages for defamation unless statements are made with reckless disregard for truth.
verdict: Permitted publication; established tort of invasion of privacy and American New York Times v. Sullivan public official standard in India.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) v. Union of India
facts: CBI report leaked widespread telephone tapping of prominent political figures by intelligence agencies. PUCL challenged arbitrary wiretapping powers under Section 5(2) of Telegraph Act.
issues: Does telephone tapping violate the right to privacy under Article 21 and freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a)?
ratio_decidendi: Telephone tapping infringes Article 21 right to privacy and Article 19(1)(a) freedom of speech unless justified under strict statutory parameters (public emergency or public safety). Formulated mandatory procedural safeguards including review committees.
verdict: Established strict telephone surveillance guidelines to prevent executive abuse.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Privacy Judgment)
facts: Retired High Court Judge K.S. Puttaswamy challenged the mandatory Aadhaar biometric identification program. The Attorney General argued that under M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1963), the Constitution guaranteed no fundamental right to privacy.
issues: Is there a fundamental right to privacy under the Indian Constitution?
Are M.P. Sharma (8 judges) and Kharak Singh (6 judges) good law?
ratio_decidendi: Privacy is an intrinsic, fundamental, and inalienable right emanating from life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the entire schema of Part III. Privacy encompasses bodily autonomy, informational privacy, and spatial privacy. Any state interference must pass the three-fold test of: (1) legality (state law), (2) legitimate state aim, and (3) proportionality.
verdict: Unanimously upheld Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right under Article 21; overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they held otherwise; explicitly denounced ADM Jabalpur.
precedents_overruled: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1963) (majority)

case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar Validity)
acts_referred: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016
facts: Substantive challenge to the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar Act, 2016, its passage as a Money Bill under Article 110, and mandatory linkage of Aadhaar to bank accounts, mobile SIM cards, school admissions, and welfare subsidies.
issues: Is the Aadhaar Act constitutionally valid under the Puttaswamy privacy proportionality test?
Was the Aadhaar Act legitimately passed as a Money Bill?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld core biometric Aadhaar for government welfare subsidies under Section 7 (legitimate state aim of preventing leakage). Struck down Section 57 allowing private corporate entities to demand Aadhaar, mandatory bank account linking, mobile SIM linking, and school admissions. Upheld passage as Money Bill (Justice Chandrachud dissented).
verdict: Partially upheld Aadhaar for welfare subsidies; prohibited private corporate exploitation of Aadhaar database.

case_name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
facts: Two girls were arrested in Maharashtra under Section 66A of the IT Act for posting comments on Facebook questioning the city shutdown for Bal Thackeray's funeral. Law student Shreya Singhal filed a PIL challenging Section 66A.
issues: Does Section 66A IT Act violate freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a)?
Is Section 66A unconstitutionally vague and overbroad?
ratio_decidendi: Section 66A created a chilling effect on free online speech. Differentiated between discussion, advocacy, and incitement. A speech becomes restriction-worthy under Article 19(2) only when it reaches the level of incitement. The terms 'grossly offensive' and 'annoying' were hopelessly vague. Read down Section 79 intermediary guidelines to require court orders or government notifications for takedowns.
verdict: Struck down Section 66A IT Act in its entirety as unconstitutional; protected internet freedom in India.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
facts: Following the revocation of Article 370 in August 2019, the government imposed indefinite internet shutdown and movement restrictions under Section 144 CrPC across Jammu and Kashmir. Editor of Kashmir Times challenged the blackout.
issues: Is access to the internet a fundamental right under Article 19?
Can indefinite internet blackouts be imposed under Telecom Suspension Rules?
ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)) and freedom to carry on trade/business (Article 19(1)(g)) using the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected fundamental rights. Indefinite internet suspensions are impermissible. All shutdown orders must satisfy proportionality and must be published proactively for judicial review.
verdict: Declared internet access constitutionally protected; prohibited indefinite shutdowns; mandated periodic review.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: State of Madras v. Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan
facts: Madras Government issued a Communal G.O. allocating medical and engineering college seats based strictly on caste and religious quotas. Brahmin student Champakam Dorairajan challenged the order after denial of admission.
issues: Does the Communal G.O. violate Article 15(1) and Article 29(2)?
Can Directive Principle Article 46 override Fundamental Rights?
ratio_decidendi: Fundamental Rights are sacrosanct and cannot be overridden by Directive Principles in Part IV. The Communal G.O. classified candidates solely on religion and caste, directly violating Article 29(2).
verdict: Struck down Communal G.O.; prompted Parliament to enact the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserting Article 15(4).

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
facts: Senior IAS officer E.P. Royappa was transferred from the post of Chief Secretary to a newly created non-cadre post, which he challenged as arbitrary, malicious, and violative of Articles 14 and 16.
issues: What is the conceptual scope of equality under Article 14?
Does Article 14 strike down arbitrary state action?
ratio_decidendi: Formulated the revolutionary 'New Doctrine of Equality'. Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions and cannot be cribbed, cabined, and confined within traditional doctrinaire limits. Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies. Where an act is arbitrary, it implicitly involves negation of equality.
verdict: Established the anti-arbitrariness principle as the foundational bedrock of Article 14.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case)
facts: V.P. Singh government implemented the Mandal Commission report reserving 27% vacancies in central civil services for Other Backward Classes (OBCs). Petitioners challenged the policy.
issues: Is caste alone a valid criterion for identifying backward classes?
What is the maximum permissible reservation ceiling?
Does reservation extend to promotions?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4). Caste can be an acceptable starting point for identifying backwardness. Established the 'Creamy Layer' exclusion principle for advanced sections of OBCs. Imposed a strict 50% ceiling on total reservations. Stated reservation applies only to initial appointments and not to promotions.
verdict: Upheld OBC reservation with creamy layer exclusion and 50% cap; prohibited reservation in promotions.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
facts: Petitioners challenged the constitutional amendments that inserted Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B) providing reservation in promotions with consequential seniority for SCs and STs, overriding Indra Sawhney.
issues: Are constitutional amendments enabling reservation in promotion with consequential seniority valid?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld the constitutional validity of Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B). However, established three mandatory preconditions that the State must satisfy before granting reservations in promotion: (1) quantifiable data on backwardness, (2) inadequate representation in the specific service, and (3) overall administrative efficiency under Article 335.
verdict: Upheld 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th Amendments subject to quantifiable data and efficiency requirements.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
acts_referred: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006)
facts: Central Government sought reconsideration of M. Nagaraj (2006) by a 7-judge bench, arguing that requiring quantifiable data of backwardness for SCs and STs contradicted the presidential lists under Articles 341 and 342.
issues: Must the State collect quantifiable data showing backwardness for SC/ST promotions?
Does the Creamy Layer doctrine apply to SC/ST reservations in promotions?
ratio_decidendi: Modified Nagaraj: State does NOT need to collect quantifiable data on backwardness for SC/STs since their backwardness is presumed. However, affirmed that the 'Creamy Layer' doctrine applies to SCs and STs to prevent benefits from being cornered by elite sections.
verdict: Clarified that SC/ST backwardness is presumed; applied creamy layer principle to SC/ST promotions.

provenance.source: Supreme Court of India / Indian Kanoon / SCR Public Legal Records

case_name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (EWS Reservation Case)
facts: Challenge to the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 which introduced 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) excluding existing SC, ST, and SEBC beneficiaries.
issues: Does reservation based solely on economic criteria violate the Basic Structure?
Does excluding SCs/STs/OBCs from EWS violate equality?
Does breaching the 50% ceiling violate the Basic Structure?
ratio_decidendi: Majority (Justices Maheshwari, Trivedi, Pardiwala) held that economic criteria is a valid basis for affirmative classification and does not violate the Basic Structure. The 50% ceiling in Indra Sawhney applied to caste reservations under Article 16(4) and is not inflexible. CJI U.U. Lalit and Justice Bhat dissented.
verdict: Upheld the validity of the 103rd Amendment Act (10% EWS reservation) by 3:2 majority.

case_name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
acts_referred: Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949
facts: Madras Government banned entry and circulation of Romesh Thappar's left-wing weekly journal 'Cross Roads' under public safety provisions.
issues: Does freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) include freedom of circulation?
Can public order justify bans when 'public order' was not in original Article 19(2)?
ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, which is ensured through freedom of circulation. There can be no freedom of speech without freedom of circulation. Restrictions outside the specific heads in Article 19(2) are void.
verdict: Struck down the circulation ban; led to First Amendment adding 'public order' to Article 19(2).

case_name: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India

issues: Does newsprint quota and page-ceiling violate freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a)?
ratio_decidendi: Direct effect and operational consequence test: Government cannot indirectly curtail freedom of the press under the guise of regulating newsprint commerce. Freedom of the press means freedom from commercial restrictions on pagination and circulation.
verdict: Struck down the 10-page newspaper ceiling as unconstitutional.

case_name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (National Anthem Case)
acts_referred: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
facts: Three school children belonging to Jehovah's Witnesses stood respectfully when the National Anthem was sung in school assembly, but did not sing along due to conscientious religious tenets. They were expelled.
issues: Does expulsion for respectfully standing without singing the National Anthem violate Articles 19(1)(a) and 25(1)?
ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to remain silent. Standing up respectfully shows proper reverence; no law obliges any citizen to sing. Expulsion violated religious freedom (Article 25) and speech (Article 19(1)(a)).
verdict: Quashed expulsion; held our tradition teaches tolerance, our philosophy preaches tolerance, our Constitution practices tolerance.

case_name: Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar (Shirur Mutt Case)
acts_referred: Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951

issues: What is religion under Article 25?
What religious practices are constitutionally protected from state interference?
ratio_decidendi: Formulated the foundational 'Essential Religious Practices' (ERP) test. What constitutes the essential part of a religion is primarily to be ascertained with reference to the doctrines of that religion itself. Secular administrative activities are distinct from core rituals.
verdict: Established the ERP doctrine governing all Indian freedom of religion jurisprudence.

case_name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
facts: 62-year-old divorced Muslim woman Shah Bano sought maintenance from her wealthy advocate husband under Section 125 CrPC. The husband argued Muslim personal law limited maintenance to the iddat period.
issues: Does Section 125 CrPC apply to divorced Muslim women notwithstanding personal law?
Is Section 125 secular in nature?
ratio_decidendi: Section 125 CrPC is a secular, compassionate statutory measure designed to prevent destitution and vagrancy. It applies to all citizens regardless of religion. It overrides personal laws where a divorced wife is unable to maintain herself. Highlighted the necessity of a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44).
verdict: Awarded maintenance to Shah Bano; affirmed secular primacy of Section 125 CrPC.

case_name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (Triple Talaq Case)
facts: Shayara Bano challenged the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instantaneous, irrevocable Triple Talaq pronounced in a single sitting) as violative of equality, non-discrimination, and dignity.
issues: Is Talaq-e-Biddat an essential religious practice protected under Article 25?
Is instant triple talaq manifestly arbitrary under Article 14?
ratio_decidendi: Talaq-e-Biddat is not an essential religious practice in Islamic theology. Justice Nariman held that instant triple talaq allows marital breakdown at the capricious whims of the husband without reconciliation, making it 'manifestly arbitrary' and void under Article 14.
verdict: Struck down Triple Talaq by 3:2 majority as unconstitutional; established manifest arbitrariness doctrine.

case_name: Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala Temple Case)
acts_referred: Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965
facts: Rule 3(b) of the Kerala rules prohibited entry of women aged 10 to 50 (menstruating age) into the Sabarimala Ayyappa temple based on the deity's celibate nature.
issues: Does excluding women aged 10-50 violate Articles 14, 15, and 25?
Is the exclusion an essential religious practice of the denomination under Article 26?
ratio_decidendi: Devotees of Lord Ayyappa do not constitute a separate religious denomination under Article 26. Excluding women on physiological attributes like menstruation is a form of untouchability and discrimination violating dignity and equality (Articles 14, 15, 21). Essential practice must be fundamental to the core faith. (Justice Indu Malhotra dissented).
verdict: Struck down Rule 3(b); permitted entry of women of all ages to Sabarimala temple.

case_name: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
acts_referred: Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW)
facts: Social worker Bhanwari Devi was gang-raped for attempting to stop child marriage in rural Rajasthan. Women's rights groups filed a PIL seeking workplace safety guidelines in the absence of enacted legislation.
issues: Does sexual harassment at the workplace violate fundamental rights of women?
